resources.string: Loaded during deadlifts, rows, pull-ups, carries, racket swings, and other movements requiring strong or prolonged gripping. Load may increase with narrow handles, forceful pinching, prolonged static gripping, or repeated racket swings.

Moves the fingers and thumb to grip and pinch objects and transfers force from a handle into the wrist. Small joints and ligaments, flexor tendons, tendon sheaths, and pulleys share compressive and tensile loads and stabilize repeated gripping.
The region extending across the palm, thumb, finger joints, and fingertips.
Hand and grip complex

Loaded during squats, deadlifts, rows, and other movements that transfer force between the upper and lower body. Load may increase when heavy weight is handled in deep trunk flexion or when repeated twisting occurs while the trunk is flexed.

Supports the weight of the upper body while allowing the lower back to flex, extend, and rotate. The discs, facet joints, and ligaments share loads and help prevent excessive translation or bending of the lumbar vertebrae.
The lower-back region extending from just above the pelvis to below the ribs.
Lumbar spine complex

Loaded during squats, stair climbing, lunges, jumps, and landings that repeatedly flex and extend the knee. Load may increase with deep knee angles, heavy loading, repeated jumping, or rapid deceleration.

Allows the patella to track along the femoral groove and transmit quadriceps force to the lower leg. The joint surfaces, quadriceps tendon, and patellar tendon work together to extend the knee and manage landing loads.
The front of the knee, including the patella and the anterior thigh tendons above and below it.
Patellofemoral complex

Loaded during rows, pull-ups, shoulder presses, and other movements that require the chest and upper back to remain supported while the arms produce force. Load may increase when substantial weight is supported with a markedly rounded back or when unilateral rotation and heavy loading are repeatedly combined.

Allows the thoracic spine to flex, extend, and rotate while allowing the ribs to move with breathing and arm motion. The thoracic vertebrae, rib joints, and fascia help transfer force between the arms and trunk and distribute loading.
The back and ribcage region extending from below the neck to the lower ribs, including the area between the shoulder blades and around the chest.
Thoracic spine and ribcage complex

Loaded during running, jumping, calf raises, footwork, and changes of direction involving push-off and landing through the ankle. Load may increase with repeated rapid landings or when the ankle is suddenly forced into twisting or extreme positions.

Transfers body weight between the lower leg and foot while allowing ankle and hindfoot motion. The joints, tendons, and medial and lateral ligaments absorb landing loads and stabilize the foot during uneven-ground contact and changes of direction.
The region extending from the medial and lateral malleoli below the lower leg to the heel and deeper structures of the ankle and hindfoot.
Ankle and hindfoot complex

Loaded during push-ups, presses, rows, curls, racket swings, and other movements where the wrist supports body weight or force from an implement. Load may increase when substantial force is applied with the wrist highly bent or when strong rotational loading is repeated.

Allows wrist flexion, extension, and side-to-side motion while transmitting force from the hand into the forearm. The joints, TFCC, intercarpal ligaments, and wrist flexor and extensor tendons share compression and torsional loading and stabilize the wrist during gripping.
The region around the wrist crease between the forearm and palm, where multiple small carpal bones are grouped together.
Wrist and carpal complex

Loaded during dumbbell curls, rows, racket swings, pronation/supination exercises, and other gripping movements that change palm orientation. Load may increase when heavy implements are rotated rapidly with a strong grip or when end-range forearm rotation is repeated.

Allows the radius to rotate around the ulna to turn the palm up or down. The proximal and distal radioulnar joints and annular ligament maintain alignment during rotation and transmit torsional force between the hand and elbow.
The forearm region extending from just below the elbow to just above the wrist, where the radius and ulna meet at both ends.
Radioulnar rotation complex

Loaded during lunges, step-ups, single-leg RDLs, lateral movement, and other tasks that place different forces on each side of the pelvis. Load may increase with large unilateral loads or repeated pelvic torsion during wide-stride movements.

Transfers force from the upper body into both legs and helps maintain pelvic stability during walking and single-leg support. The posterior sacroiliac joints and anterior pubic symphysis share compression and torsional loading.
The ring-shaped region extending from the back of the pelvis just below the lower back to the front of the pelvis below the lower abdomen.
Pelvic ring and sacroiliac complex

Loaded during presses, rows, pull-ups, racket swings, and other movements that push, pull, or use the arm overhead. Load may increase when heavy weight is controlled near end range or when rapid overhead rotation and deceleration are repeated.

Allows large arm movements in multiple directions while helping the humeral head remain centered in the joint. The articular surfaces, rotator cuff, labrum, capsule, and tendons share pushing, pulling, and rotational loads.
The deep shoulder region where the glenoid of the scapula meets the head of the humerus.
Glenohumeral complex

Loaded during squats, lunges, step-ups, running, and changes of direction where the knee accepts body weight. Load may increase when deep knee angles, heavy loading, rapid deceleration, or twisting occur together.

Flexes and extends the knee while transferring body weight and external load from the thigh to the lower leg. The articular surfaces, menisci, tendons, and ligaments share impact and support front-to-back, side-to-side, and rotational alignment.
The main knee-joint region where the lower femur meets the upper tibia.
Tibiofemoral complex

Loaded during squats, hinges, lunges, step-ups, and other movements involving deep hip positions or force production through one leg. Load may increase when heavy loading, deep joint angles, and rapid changes of direction occur together.

Moves the leg forward, backward, laterally, and through rotation while transferring body weight and external load between the pelvis and leg. The joint, capsule, ligaments, and surrounding tendons support large ranges of motion and help stabilize the pelvis during single-leg support.
The connection between the pelvis and femur, spanning the deep groin and the front, side, and back of the hip.
Hip complex

Loaded during overhead exercise, swimming, smashes, and other movements that require head support while the arms move through a large range. Load may increase when high force is produced with a forward-head position or when end-range extension and rotation are repeated.

Supports the weight of the head while allowing the neck to flex, extend, and rotate. The discs, facet joints, and ligaments share loads and help prevent excessive translation or bending of the cervical vertebrae.
The entire neck region extending from below the head to above the shoulders.
Cervical spine complex

Loaded during curls, rows, pull-ups, push-ups, presses, throws, and other movements involving repeated elbow flexion and extension. Load may increase when heavy weight is supported near end range or during repeated high-speed swinging or throwing actions.

Flexes and extends the elbow while transferring pushing and pulling forces between the upper arm and forearm. The articular surfaces, biceps and triceps tendons, and collateral ligaments share loading and help resist excessive side-to-side or rotational motion.
The front, back, medial, and lateral regions of the elbow where the upper arm meets the forearm.
Elbow flexion-extension complex

Loaded during running, jumping, calf raises, footwork, and other movements that press through the ball of the foot and toes. Load may increase with repeated forceful push-offs or when body weight is applied through a twisted foot.

Transfers body weight from the heel toward the toes and allows push-off through the forefoot. Small joints, the plantar fascia, toe tendons, and ligaments support the arch and distribute landing impact and torsional loading.
The front portion of the foot extending from the midfoot arch to the ball of the foot and the bases of the toes.
Midfoot and forefoot complex

Loaded during rows, push-ups, pull-ups, shoulder presses, and other movements that require coordinated scapular and clavicular motion. Load may increase when heavy repetitions are performed with the scapula elevated or tilted to one side.

Allows the scapula to glide and rotate over the ribcage so the arm can move overhead. The clavicular joints and ligaments transfer force from the arm to the trunk and help maintain shoulder-girdle alignment.
The shoulder-girdle region formed by the scapula in the upper back and the clavicle across the upper chest.
Scapuloclavicular complex

Loaded during rows, push-ups, pull-ups, shoulder presses, and other movements that retract, protract, or upwardly rotate the scapula. Load may increase when repetitions are performed with the scapula persistently elevated or tilted to one side.
Allows the scapula to move up, down, forward, backward, and rotate so the arm can reach overhead. It transfers force from the arm into the trunk and provides a stable base for shoulder-joint motion.
The region in the upper back where the broad anterior surface of the scapula glides over the posterior ribcage.
Scapulothoracic functional articulation

Loaded during lunges, step-ups, single-leg RDLs, and other movements that place different forces on the two sides of the pelvis. Load may increase with heavy unilateral loading or rapid changes of direction that increase pelvic torsion.
Helps prevent excessive separation or sliding of the sacroiliac joint and supports the pelvis as force transfers between the upper body and legs. It also limits excessive sudden torsion.
Strong ligaments around the dimples of the lower back that connect the sacrum to the pelvic bones.
Sacroiliac ligament complex

Loaded during rows, curls, carries, racket swings, and other movements that require a strong grip with the wrist held stable. Load may increase when prolonged gripping or repeated wrist extension is performed under substantial load.
Transfers force from the forearm muscles to extend the wrist and fingers and helps keep the wrist neutral during strong gripping. It also controls wrist flexion as objects are lowered.
Tendons running from the posterior-lateral forearm across the back of the wrist into the hand.
Wrist extensor tendon complex

Loaded during push-ups, throws, smashes, and other movements where an extended elbow accepts body weight or rapid rotation. Load may increase when the hand is planted while the body rotates or when the elbow is forced into excessive lockout.
Helps prevent excessive opening of the lateral elbow or inward angling of the forearm. It also limits rotatory displacement of the joint when the elbow is extended.
Ligament structures on the outside of the elbow connecting the humerus to the forearm and wrapping around the posterolateral joint.
Elbow lateral collateral ligament complex

Loaded during A-skips, running, wall drives, and other movements involving repeated lifting of the forefoot. Load may increase when these anterior ankle movements continue over long distances or at high repetition rates.

Transfers force from the anterior lower-leg muscle to lift the forefoot and control how quickly the foot lowers to the ground during landing. It also helps prevent the foot from catching the ground during running.
A tendon extending from the anterolateral lower-leg muscle across the front of the ankle to the medial top of the foot.
Anterior tibial tendon

Loaded during curls, chin-ups, rows, and other movements that combine elbow flexion with supination or pulling. Load may increase when a heavy object is suddenly caught or pulled while the elbow is nearly extended.
Transfers biceps force to flex the elbow and turn the palm upward. It also controls the rate of elbow extension while a weight is lowered.
A thick tendon at the front of the elbow connecting the anterior upper-arm muscle to the radius on the thumb side of the forearm.
Distal biceps tendon

Loaded during push-ups, bench presses, shoulder presses, pull-ups, and other pushing and pulling movements. Load may increase when heavy loads are used with the arm elevated or when direct pressure is applied to the top of the shoulder for prolonged periods.
Coordinates clavicular and scapular motion as the arm is raised and distributes forces transferred from the arm to the trunk. It helps guide upward rotation and tilting of the scapula.
A small joint at the top of the shoulder where the outer end of the clavicle meets the acromion of the scapula.
Acromioclavicular joint

Loaded during single-leg calf raises, running, footwork, and other movements that require maintaining the foot arch while pushing against the ground. Load may increase when the foot repeatedly collapses inward or when changes of direction and landings are repeated.
Transfers force from the deep calf muscles to the medial foot to support the arch and limit excessive inward collapse of the foot. It stabilizes the ankle during single-leg support and push-off.
A tendon that begins in the deep posteromedial lower leg, passes behind the medial malleolus, and continues into the medial arch of the foot.
Posterior tibial tendon

Loaded during RDLs, deadlifts, hip hinges, fast running, and other movements involving hip flexion and extension. Load may increase when the trunk bends deeply with the knees relatively straight or when the hamstrings contract forcefully immediately after rapid lengthening.
Transfers hamstring force to the pelvis to extend the hip and control knee motion. It is lengthened during running and hip-hinge movements and also accepts force during deceleration.
Tendons extending from the sitting-bone region near the gluteal fold into the muscles of the back of the thigh.
Proximal hamstring tendon complex
Loaded during calf raises, running, jumping, landing, and rebounding movements. Load may increase with repeated rapid jumps or repeated sudden acceleration.
Transfers calf-muscle force to the heel to push against the ground. During running and jumping, it also lengthens to store force and then helps return that force.
A thick tendon extending from the muscles at the back of the lower leg to the heel bone.
Achilles tendon

Loaded during presses, rows, pull-ups, push-ups, and other movements requiring coordinated scapular and clavicular motion. Load may increase when heavy loads strongly depress the shoulder or when the arm is repeatedly raised to end range.
Provides the clavicle\'s only bony connection to the trunk and transfers forces from the arm and shoulder into the torso. It guides clavicular elevation and rotation as the arm moves up and down.
The joint at the center of the upper chest where the inner end of the clavicle meets the upper sternum.
Sternoclavicular joint

Loaded during step-ups, lunges, single-leg RDLs, lateral walking, and other movements that require the pelvis to be supported on one leg. Load may increase with high repetition or repeated pelvic drop.
Transfers force from the lateral hip muscles to abduct the leg and keep the pelvis level during single-leg support. It also helps control excessive inward movement of the hip.
Tendons around the bony prominence on the outside of the hip that connect the lateral pelvic muscles to the femur.
Gluteus medius-minimus tendon complex

Loaded during lateral lunges, hip-adduction work, shuttle pickup, changes of direction, and other movements that repeatedly move the leg outward and back inward. Load may increase with rapid direction changes from a wide stance or repeated work under fatigue.
Transfers force from the inner-thigh muscles to bring the leg toward the body and control the pelvis and leg during lateral movement. It also helps pull a widely abducted leg back toward the body.
Tendon structures along the groin and inner thigh connecting the pelvis to the femur.
Adductor tendon complex

Loaded during landings, sudden stops, rapid changes of direction, and other movements that abruptly redirect the body. Load may increase when the knee collapses inward while the trunk and foot are oriented in different directions.
Helps prevent the tibia from translating too far forward relative to the femur and limits excessive knee rotation during sudden stops and changes of direction.
A ligament deep inside the knee that runs diagonally between the femur and tibia.
Anterior cruciate ligament

Loaded during rows, pull-ups, lateral raises, shoulder presses, and other movements involving lifting or pulling the arm. Load may increase when a loaded arm is held far from the body or when rapid overhead actions and deceleration are repeated.
Transfers rotator-cuff force to the humerus to externally rotate and elevate the arm. It also helps keep the humeral head centered in the joint as the arm moves.
Tendons extending from muscles on the upper and posterior scapula around the upper part of the humerus.
Posterosuperior rotator cuff tendon complex

Loaded during rows, pull-ups, shoulder presses, and other movements that require an upright chest or a stable trunk. Load may increase when weight is lifted with strong thoracic extension or when extension and rotation are repeatedly combined.
Guides motion during thoracic extension and rotation and allows the ribs to move with breathing and arm motion. It also distributes posterior loading across multiple joints.
Small joints in the upper back where adjacent thoracic vertebrae meet and where the ribs articulate with the thoracic spine.
Thoracic facet and costovertebral joint complex

Loaded during B-stance RDLs, step-ups, lunges, and other movements that place more body weight on one leg. Load may increase with large unilateral loads or repeated movement with the pelvis in a twisted position.
Transfers force from the upper body into both legs and permits small pelvic movements during walking and single-leg tasks. It distributes load when force differs between the two sides of the pelvis.
The joints where the sacrum meets the pelvis, located deep to the dimples on either side of the lower back.
Sacroiliac joint complex

Loaded during pull-ups, lat pulldowns, rows, pullovers, and other movements that pull the arm down from overhead or backward. Load may increase when a heavy load is pulled rapidly with the arm extended far overhead.
Transfers force from the back muscles to the humerus to pull the arm downward, backward, and toward the trunk. It transmits large pulling forces between the trunk and arm.
Tendon structures at the back of the armpit where back muscles connect to the upper inner humerus.
Latissimus dorsi-teres major tendon complex

Loaded during deep squats, lunges, leg presses, and other movements that use large ranges of hip flexion or extension. Load may increase when knee and foot alignment diverge in deep positions or when end-range rotation is repeatedly used.
Helps keep the femoral head within the joint while allowing normal hip flexion, extension, and rotation. It limits excessive separation and rotation as the leg approaches end range.
Deep around the hip joint, forming a sleeve-like structure that surrounds the joint and connects the pelvis to the femur.
Hip capsuloligamentous complex

Loaded during curls, rows, pull-ups, wrist curls, and other movements involving strong gripping, wrist flexion, or forearm pronation. Load may increase when strong gripping and repeated pronation continue for prolonged periods.
Transfers force from muscles that flex the wrist and fingers and pronate the forearm. It also supports the medial side of the wrist and forearm during strong gripping.
The tendon region around the bony prominence on the inside of the elbow where the anterior forearm muscles continue toward the wrist and fingers.
Common flexor-pronator tendon complex

Loaded during overhead extensions, smashes, medicine-ball slams, and other movements that require neck support while the arms work overhead. Load may increase when high force is produced with a forward-head position or when substantial neck extension and rapid rotation are repeated.

Distributes weight and impact from the head and upper body across the cervical vertebrae while allowing the neck to flex, extend, and rotate. It also guides motion and helps limit excessive translation between vertebrae.
Deep in the back of the neck, between the cervical vertebrae and along the surfaces where adjacent vertebrae meet.
Cervical disc-endplate complex

Loaded during single-leg calf raises, running, footwork, changes of direction, and other movements that control inward and outward tilting of the foot. Load may increase with repeated unstable landings or rapid lateral transitions.
Allows the sole of the foot to tilt inward and outward to adapt to uneven ground and changes of direction. It distributes rotational force and impact from the leg into the foot.
A joint deep below the ankle around the inner heel, where the talus meets the calcaneus.
Subtalar joint

Loaded during leg curls, running, single-leg landings, and changes of direction that require knee flexion and lateral stabilization. Load may increase with repeated rapid deceleration or tibial rotation.
Transfers hamstring force to flex the knee and control external rotation of the lower leg. It also helps stabilize the lateral knee during single-leg movements.
A tendon at the posterolateral knee connecting the hamstring muscles to the upper lateral fibula.
Distal biceps femoris tendon

Loaded during push-ups, bench presses, dips, triceps extensions, and other movements requiring forceful elbow extension. Load may increase when heavy weight is pushed rapidly or repeatedly from deep elbow flexion.
Transfers triceps force to extend the elbow and push away. It controls elbow flexion while lowering weight and stabilizes the end of pressing movements.
A tendon at the back of the elbow connecting the posterior upper-arm muscle to the pointed olecranon of the elbow.
Distal triceps tendon

Loaded during racket swings, medicine-ball catches, farmer\'s carries, and other movements where the thumb presses against a handle or object. Load may increase when thick or slippery handles are gripped forcefully and repeatedly.

Transfers force from muscles that abduct, extend, and flex the thumb, allowing pinching and wrapping the thumb around a handle. It stabilizes the thumb side of the grip when holding rackets and dumbbells.
Multiple tendons extending from the thumb side of the wrist to the base and distal segments of the thumb.
Thumb tendon complex

Loaded during rows, pull-ups, lat pulldowns, and other movements involving elbow flexion while pulling or using the arm overhead. Load may increase with forceful pulling while the arm is elevated or with high volumes of repeated overhead movement.
Transfers biceps force toward the shoulder and helps stabilize the front-superior humeral head while the arm is lifted or pulling. It repeatedly glides within its groove as the arm moves.
A slender tendon at the front of the shoulder that passes through the groove of the humerus and continues into the upper part of the shoulder joint.
Long-head biceps tendon

Loaded during deadlifts, rows, pull-ups, carries, and other movements involving strong whole-hand gripping of heavy handles. Load may increase when a strong grip is maintained for prolonged periods or when the fingers accept load while twisted.

Allows the finger joints to conform to the shape of an object while preventing them from shifting excessively under grip force. It distributes compression and torsion across multiple joints of the hand.
Ligament structures connecting the small bones and joints throughout the palm and finger joints.
Hand-grip joint-ligament complex

Loaded during calf raises, squats, running, landings, and other movements involving ankle flexion and extension. Load may increase with heavy loading in deep ankle dorsiflexion or repeated firm landings.
Allows the ankle to move up and down and transfers body weight into the foot during standing and landing. It guides motion between the lower leg and foot while distributing impact.
The deep anterior ankle joint where the talus sits between the lower ends of the tibia and fibula.
Talocrural joint

Loaded during rows, pull-ups, shoulder presses, and other movements that transfer force through the upper back and shoulders. Load may increase when heavy weight is supported with a markedly rounded upper back or when a twisted posture is repeatedly maintained.

Distributes upper-body weight and forces from the arms across the thoracic vertebrae while allowing the upper back to flex, extend, and rotate. Together with the ribs, it helps maintain smooth trunk movement.
Between the thoracic vertebrae in the region between the shoulder blades and along the surfaces where adjacent vertebrae meet.
Thoracic disc-endplate complex

Loaded during landings, lunges, changes of direction, and other movements that transfer large forces through the medial ankle. Load may increase when the foot suddenly tilts outward while the lower leg rotates.
Strongly connects the medial ankle and helps prevent excessive outward tilting or separation of the foot. It also supports lower-leg and foot alignment during loaded rotational movements.
A fan-shaped ligament complex extending from the medial malleolus to the medial talus and calcaneus.
Ankle deltoid ligament complex

Loaded during deep squats, lunges, deeply flexed leg presses, and other movements that apply posterior force to the tibia. Load may increase with heavy loading at deep knee angles or when impact is applied to the front of the knee.

Helps prevent the tibia from translating too far backward relative to the femur and maintains front-to-back joint alignment during deep knee flexion. It also supports the center of the knee during rotation.
A ligament deep inside the knee that runs behind the ACL and connects the femur to the tibia.
Posterior cruciate ligament

Loaded during calf raises, running, jumping, and other movements involving toe extension and push-off through the forefoot. Load may increase with repeated barefoot impact, prolonged repetitive loading, or rapid changes of direction that repeatedly stretch the arch.
Supports the foot arch and distributes tension between the heel and toes to transfer force during walking and running. It tightens as the toes extend, helping the foot become a firm lever.
A thick fascial structure running along the sole of the foot from the heel bone to the bases of the toes.
Plantar fascia complex

Loaded during bench presses, push-ups, flyes, dips, and other movements that press while moving the arms apart and back together. Load may increase when heavy weight is pushed rapidly from a position where the arm has moved deeply behind the body.
Transfers pectoralis-major force to the humerus to push the arm forward and bring it toward the body. It lengthens as the arm moves backward and also helps decelerate pressing movements.
A tendon extending from the large chest muscle across the front fold of the armpit to the upper humerus.
Pectoralis major tendon complex

Loaded during deadlifts, rows, curls, carries, and other movements involving strong gripping with the wrist held stable. Load may increase when a strong grip is maintained for a long time with the wrist extended backward.
Transfers force from the forearm muscles to flex the wrist and fingers and grip objects. It also stabilizes the front of the wrist against excessive extension while holding weight.
Tendons running from the anterior-medial forearm across the palm side of the wrist into the hand and fingers.
Wrist flexor tendon complex

Loaded during push-ups, bench presses, rows, pull-ups, and other movements that transfer large forces through the arm. Load may increase when a heavy load is carried by one arm or when the shoulder is strongly pulled downward.

Helps prevent excessive separation or vertical displacement between the clavicle and scapula. It stabilizes the shoulder girdle while the weight of the arm and pushing or pulling forces are transferred toward the trunk.
Ligament structures at the top of the shoulder connecting the outer clavicle with the acromion and coracoid processes of the scapula.
Acromioclavicular-coracoclavicular ligament complex

Loaded during hip abduction, footwork, lateral bounds, and other movements that require single-leg support while moving laterally. Load may increase when the pelvis repeatedly tilts or the knee repeatedly collapses inward.
Distributes tension along the lateral hip and thigh to help stabilize the pelvis and knee during single-leg support. It also transfers force during hip abduction and rapid changes of direction.
The upper portion of the broad fascial structure that begins at the front-lateral pelvis and runs down the outside of the thigh.
Proximal TFL-IT band complex

Loaded during deep lunges, landings, footwork, and other movements involving rotation or changes of direction with the ankle dorsiflexed. Load may increase when the foot remains fixed while the body suddenly rotates outward.

Maintains the spacing between the two bones so they can securely surround the talus and controls the small separation required during ankle dorsiflexion. It also limits excessive twisting when the foot rotates outward.
Ligament structures just above the ankle that bind the lower ends of the tibia and fibula together.
Distal tibiofibular syndesmosis complex

Loaded during push-ups, bench presses, shoulder presses, and other movements involving pushing or resisting internal rotation. Load may increase with repeated heavy loading or rapid pushing when the arm is positioned far behind the body.
Transfers subscapularis force to internally rotate the arm. As part of the rotator cuff, it also helps keep the humeral head centered during pushing and overhead movements.
A tendon deep in the front of the armpit connecting the muscle on the anterior surface of the scapula to the upper humerus.
Subscapularis tendon

Loaded during calf raises, running, jumping, footwork, and other movements involving push-off or landing through the ball of the foot. Load may increase with repeated forceful forefoot push-off or when body weight is accepted through a twisted foot.
Allows the arch to adapt to the ground and transfers body weight from the heel toward the toes. During walking and running, it allows the foot to become a firm lever while still distributing impact.
The joint region extending from the middle of the top of the foot to the ball of the foot just behind the toes, where multiple small bones articulate.
Midfoot and forefoot joint complex

Loaded during A-skips, footwork, running, jumping, and other movements involving rapid knee drive and extension. Load may increase when the leg is forcefully driven forward immediately after being extended far behind the body or when rapid repetitions accumulate.
Transfers rectus femoris force to help lift the leg forward and extend the knee. It transfers force across both the hip and knee during rapid running and jumping actions.
A tendon at the front of the pelvis, extending from just below the anterior pelvic prominence into the front of the thigh.
Proximal rectus femoris tendon complex

Loaded during landings, footwork, lateral bounds, and other movements where body weight is accepted through the heel while resisting lateral motion. Load may increase when body weight is applied while the entire foot is tilted inward.
Helps prevent excessive inward tilting of the ankle and heel and supports the lateral ankle in neutral and dorsiflexed positions. It also limits excessive tilting at the subtalar joint.
A ligament running downward from the lateral malleolus to the outer side of the calcaneus.
Calcaneofibular ligament

Loaded during lunges, single-leg landings, rapid changes of direction, and other movements requiring lateral knee stability. Load may increase when the foot is fixed and the knee angles outward while rotation occurs.
Helps prevent excessive opening of the lateral knee and excessive outward angling of the knee. It also limits excessive tibial rotation and posterolateral translation.
Ligament structures along the outside and posterolateral aspect of the knee, connecting the femur with the upper fibula and surrounding the back-outside of the knee.
Lateral collateral and posterolateral complex

Loaded during overhead presses, swimming, kettlebell halos, and other large arm movements performed while maintaining neck position. Load may increase when weight is supported with the neck at end-range extension or when extension and rotation occur together.
Guides motion during neck extension, side bending, and rotation. It also distributes pressure between vertebrae and helps limit excessive sliding.
Small joints on both sides of the back of the neck where adjacent cervical vertebrae meet.
Cervical facet joint complex

Loaded during squats, lunges, step-ups, leg extensions, and other movements involving repeated knee flexion and extension. Load may increase when deep knee angles and heavy loading are combined or when repetition volume becomes high.
Guides the patella along its groove so force from the anterior thigh muscles can be transferred efficiently. It also distributes pressure generated during knee flexion across a broader area.
The joint at the front of the knee where the back of the patella contacts the groove on the front of the femur.
Patellofemoral joint

Loaded during leg curls, single-leg landings, footwork, and other movements involving knee flexion or medial knee stabilization. Load may increase when rapid deceleration and rotation occur together or when these movements are repeated under fatigue.

Transfers force from the posterior and medial thigh muscles to flex the knee and control tibial rotation. It also contributes to medial knee stability during single-leg landing and changes of direction.
Tendons at the back-medial knee where the posterior and medial thigh muscles connect to the upper tibia.
Distal medial hamstring and gracilis tendon complex

Loaded during pull-ups, shoulder presses, pullovers, and other movements involving overhead lifting or forceful pulling. Load may increase when the arm is pulled while twisting near end range or when rapid overhead movements are repeated.

Deepens the shallow shoulder socket to help the humeral head remain centered. It distributes compression and tensile forces around the joint margin and also provides attachment for several ligaments and tendons.
A ring of fibrocartilage surrounding the edge of the shallow glenoid socket deep within the shoulder.
Glenoid labrum

Loaded during pull-ups, shoulder presses, pullovers, and other movements that take the arm through large overhead or behind-the-body ranges. Load may increase when heavy weight is held for prolonged periods near end range or when the arm rotates rapidly.

Allows the shoulder\'s large range of motion while helping prevent excessive translation or separation of the humeral head from the joint. It limits excessive rotation and separation as the arm approaches end range.
A deep shoulder structure that surrounds the joint like a sleeve and connects the scapula to the humerus.
Glenohumeral capsuloligamentous complex

Loaded during deadlifts, good mornings, barbell rows, and other movements that require supporting weight with the trunk flexed. Load may increase when the lower back rounds substantially under heavy load or when twisting is added to a flexed position.

Lengthens during lumbar flexion and helps prevent excessive separation or front-to-back translation between vertebrae. It also contributes to posterior lumbar stability while load is supported in a flexed position.
Ligament structures running along the back of the lower lumbar spine just above the pelvis.
Lumbar posterior ligament complex

Loaded during smashes, tennis serves, medicine-ball throws, and other rapid arm-swinging movements. Load may increase when the arm accelerates forcefully while the elbow trails behind the body or when high repetition volumes accumulate.
Helps prevent excessive opening of the medial elbow and resists valgus stress during throwing and smashes. It also supports elbow alignment during rotation.
A ligament complex on the inside of the elbow connecting the humerus to the ulna on the little-finger side of the forearm.
Elbow medial collateral ligament complex

Loaded during curls, rows, pull-ups, push-ups, presses, and other movements involving repeated elbow flexion and extension. Load may increase when heavy weight is held at full lockout or when rapid flexion and extension are repeated.

Allows elbow flexion and extension and transfers pushing and pulling forces between the upper arm and forearm. Its articular surfaces distribute pressure and impact while guiding the forearm along a stable path.
The hinge-like joint at the center of the elbow where the lower humerus meets the two forearm bones.
Elbow flexion-extension joint complex

Loaded during deadlifts, bridges, step-ups, squats, and other movements involving forceful hip extension. Load may increase with repeated heavy loading or when the pelvis repeatedly shifts during single-leg work.
Transfers gluteus maximus force into the pelvis and femur to raise the body and drive force into the ground. It also contributes to pelvic and hip stability during single-leg support.
Tendon region extending from the large muscle at the back of the hip to the upper femur and the lateral fascial structures of the thigh.
Gluteus maximus tendon complex

Loaded during squats, lunges, deadlifts, step-ups, and other movements involving deep hip positions or forceful pushing through the legs. Load may increase when heavy loading, deep joint angles, and single-leg support occur together.

Allows the leg to move forward, backward, laterally, and through rotation while distributing body weight and external load between the pelvis and leg. The rounded joint surfaces help maintain joint alignment through large ranges of motion.
Deep in the groin, where the head of the femur meets the socket of the pelvis.
Hip joint

Loaded during squats, lunges, step-ups, and other movements involving knee flexion under body weight. Load may increase when the foot remains planted while the body twists in a deep knee position or during rapid changes of direction.

Distributes body weight and impact across a wider area and helps the rounded femoral surfaces move stably over the tibia. It also helps maintain joint-surface alignment during knee flexion and rotation.
Crescent-shaped fibrocartilage structures deep inside the knee between the femur and tibia.
Knee meniscal complex

Loaded during rows, pull-ups, curls, wrist extensions, and other movements involving strong gripping with the wrist held stable. Load may increase when heavy objects are held for prolonged periods with the wrist bent or when repeated supination accumulates.
Transfers force from muscles that extend the wrist and fingers and supinate the forearm. It also helps keep the wrist from collapsing forward during gripping.
The tendon region around the bony prominence on the outside of the elbow where the posterior forearm muscles continue toward the wrist and fingers.
Common extensor-supinator tendon complex

Loaded during push-ups, bench presses, shoulder presses, and other movements that transfer force through a neutral or extended wrist. Load may increase when heavy loading or repeated impact occurs with the wrist in substantial extension.
Helps the small carpal bones move together without excessive separation or displacement. It maintains alignment between the bones when force is accepted through the palm or the wrist bends.
Short ligament structures deep in the center of the wrist connecting adjacent carpal bones.
Scapholunate-lunotriquetral ligament complex

Loaded during squats, lunges, step-ups, leg presses, and other movements involving loaded knee flexion and extension. Load may increase when heavy loading, deep knee angles, rapid deceleration, or twisting occur together.
Transfers body weight and external load from the thigh to the lower leg while allowing knee flexion and extension. The joint surfaces and menisci guide motion and distribute pressure and impact.
The main joint deep in the knee where the lower femur meets the upper tibia.
Tibiofemoral joint

Loaded during deadlifts, rows, pull-ups, carries, and other movements requiring prolonged gripping of a bar or weight with the fingers. Load may increase with narrow handles, forceful gripping, or long periods of repeated grip work.
Transfers forearm-muscle force into the fingers for gripping and allows the tendons to glide smoothly along each finger. The pulleys keep the tendons close to the bones as the fingers flex.
Flexor tendons running from the palm along the inner side of the fingers to the fingertips, together with ring-like pulleys that hold the tendons close to the bones.
Finger flexor tendon-pulley complex

Loaded during lateral lunges, hip adduction/abduction work, footwork, and other movements that spread the legs or push forcefully to one side. Load may increase with repeated wide steps and rapid side-to-side transitions.

Connects the two sides of the pelvis anteriorly and distributes forces generated during walking and single-leg support. It permits small movements while helping absorb loading as the pelvis separates or twists.
A fibrocartilaginous joint at the front-center of the pelvis, just below the lower abdomen, connecting the left and right pubic bones.
Pubic symphysis fibrocartilage complex

Loaded during dumbbell curls, rows, pronation/supination exercises, and other movements that lift weight while changing palm orientation. Load may increase when heavy implements are rotated rapidly with a strong grip or when end-range rotation is repeated.
Allows the radius to rotate around the ulna to turn the palm up and down. It distributes compression and torsion generated during rotation between the elbow and wrist.
The two joints where the radius and ulna meet just below the elbow and just above the wrist.
Proximal-distal radioulnar joint complex

Loaded during medicine-ball slams, swimming, kettlebell halos, and other movements that require the neck to stabilize or move with arm action. Load may increase with prolonged deep neck flexion or repeated rapid flexion and rotation.
Lengthens during neck flexion and helps prevent excessive separation or front-to-back translation between vertebrae. It also supports posterior neck stability during sudden bending or rotation.
Ligament structures running along the midline of the back of the neck and connecting adjacent cervical vertebrae.
Cervical posterior ligament complex

Loaded during lateral raises, shoulder presses, bench presses, and other movements involving lifting or pushing the arm. Load may increase when heavy weight is lifted with the arm held far from the body or when rapid repetitions accumulate.
Transfers deltoid force to the humerus to raise the arm forward and sideways and move it backward. It helps control arm position during pressing and lifting movements.
The tendon region extending from the muscle covering the shoulder to the middle of the lateral humerus.
Deltoid tendon complex

Loaded during calf raises, running, jumping, and other movements that place body weight on the forefoot while extending the toes. Load may increase when a raised-heel position or repeated forceful push-off is sustained.
Supports body weight beneath the toe joints and helps prevent excessive upward extension of the toes. It helps maintain toe-joint stability during push-off.
A firm fibrocartilaginous structure beneath the bases of the toes, connecting the metatarsal heads with the proximal toe bones.
Metatarsophalangeal plantar plate complex

Loaded during A-skips, high-knee drills, footwork, and other movements involving repeated high knee lift. Load may increase when deep hip extension from a long stride is immediately followed by rapid hip flexion.
Transfers iliopsoas force to the femur to lift the leg forward and advance the leg during walking and running. It passes across the front of the hip and supports repeated hip-flexion movement.
A deep tendon running through the lower abdomen and groin from the pelvis to the inner upper femur.
Iliopsoas tendon complex

Loaded during rows, pull-ups, push-ups, shoulder presses, and other movements involving pushing, pulling, or lifting the arm overhead. Load may increase when heavy weight is controlled near end range or when rapid rotation is repeated.

Provides a large range of motion for lifting and rotating the arm in multiple directions. With support from the rotator cuff and glenoid labrum, it guides the humeral head as it moves within the center of the joint.
The deep shoulder joint where the rounded head of the humerus meets the shallow socket of the scapula.
Glenohumeral joint

Loaded during squats, lunges, jumps, landings, leg extensions, and other movements requiring rapid knee extension or control of knee flexion. Load may increase with repeated jumping, rapid deceleration, or heavy loading.
Transfers force from the anterior thigh muscles to the tibia to extend the knee and push against the ground. It lengthens during jumping and landing, helping store force and absorb loading.
A tendon at the front of the knee connecting the bottom of the patella to the upper tibia.
Patellar tendon

Loaded during deadlifts, RDLs, squats, rows, and other movements that transfer force between the upper and lower body through the lower back. Load may increase when the lower back becomes markedly rounded under heavy load or when flexion and twisting occur together.
Distributes upper-body and external loads across the lower lumbar spine while allowing lumbar flexion and extension. It absorbs loading between vertebrae and helps limit excessive translation.
In the lower back just above the pelvis, between the lowest lumbar vertebrae and the sacrum, including the discs and adjacent vertebral endplates.
Lumbar disc-endplate complex (L4-S1)

Loaded during rows, curls, push-ups, presses, and other movements involving gripping weight or pushing through the palm. Load may increase when substantial force is applied with the wrist highly bent or when repeated impacts occur.

Allows the wrist to flex, extend, and move side to side while distributing force from the hand into the forearm. Multiple small bones move together to prevent the wrist from bending at a single point.
The joints in the center of the wrist where the forearm bones meet the carpal bones and where the carpal bones meet one another.
Radiocarpal-midcarpal joint complex

Loaded during single-leg calf raises, footwork, lateral bounds, changes of direction, and other movements requiring lateral ankle control. Load may increase when the foot rapidly tilts inward or when repeated landings accumulate.

Transfers force from the lateral lower-leg muscles into the foot and helps control sudden inward rolling of the ankle. It supports lateral ankle stability during single-leg landings and lateral movement.
Tendons that begin along the outside of the lower leg, pass behind the lateral malleolus, and continue into the lateral and plantar aspects of the foot.
Peroneal tendon complex

Loaded during curls, rows, pronation/supination exercises, and other pulling movements involving forearm rotation. Load may increase with forceful twisting while the elbow is extended or with repeated rotation under heavy load.
Holds the radial head in position while allowing it to rotate smoothly. It helps limit excessive translation or separation as the palm turns up and down.
A ligament deep on the outside of the elbow that forms a ring around the head of the radius.
Radial annular ligament

Loaded during jump landings, line hops, footwork, and other movements where the ankle can tilt rapidly. Load may increase when landing on the outside of the foot with the toes pointed down or when inward rolling and rotation occur together.

When the foot is pointed downward, it helps limit excessive inward rolling of the ankle and excessive forward movement of the talus. It also supports lateral stability during rapid changes of direction.
A ligament running across the front of the lateral ankle from the lateral malleolus to the talus.
Anterior talofibular ligament

Loaded during deadlifts, RDLs, rows, unilateral lifting, and other movements that transfer force between the upper and lower body or across the two sides of the body. Load may increase with heavy unilateral loading or repeated twisting while bent forward.
Transfers force among the back, abdominal, and hip regions to support the trunk. During unilateral arm or leg actions, it helps distribute tension across the opposite side of the trunk and pelvis.
A broad, dense fascial structure covering the lower back and linking the lower ribs, spine, and pelvis.
Thoracolumbar fascia load unit

Loaded during squats, lunges, leg extensions, jumps, landings, and other movements requiring forceful knee extension or control of knee flexion. Load may increase with heavy loading or repeated rapid landings.
Transfers quadriceps force to the patella to extend the knee and control knee flexion during landing. It also contributes to rapid loading and force production during jumping and running.
A thick tendon at the front of the knee connecting the anterior thigh muscles to the upper part of the patella.
Quadriceps tendon

Loaded during calf raises, running, jumping, footwork, and other movements involving pressing the toes into the ground during push-off. Load may increase with forceful toe gripping and repeated jumping.
Transfers force from the toe-flexor muscles to grip the ground and push off through the forefoot. It also contributes to arch support and single-leg balance.
Tendons that begin deep in the lower leg, pass behind the ankle and through the sole, and continue to the ends of the toes.
Toe flexor tendon complex

Loaded during running, jumping, changes of direction, and other movements that place body weight through the midfoot while pushing off through the forefoot. Load may increase when large force is applied while the foot is plantarflexed or twisted.
Helps prevent the midfoot bones from separating or shifting and allows the arch to support body weight. It helps keep the midfoot rigid as force moves from the heel toward the toes.
A deep ligament structure in the middle of the top of the foot connecting the small tarsal bones to the base of the second metatarsal.
Lisfranc ligament complex

Loaded during push-ups, pronation/supination exercises, racket swings, and other movements that place body weight through the wrist or rotate the forearm. Load may increase when strong twisting occurs with the wrist deviated toward the little-finger side.

Distributes compression and torsional loading through the ulnar side of the wrist and stabilizes the distal ends of the two forearm bones. It helps maintain joint alignment during forearm rotation and side-to-side wrist motion.
A fibrocartilage and ligament complex on the little-finger side of the wrist between the distal forearm bones and the carpal bones.
Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC)

Loaded during lunges, step-ups, footwork, and other movements that place body weight on one leg. Load may increase when the foot is fixed and the knee collapses inward or when force is applied from the outside.
Helps prevent excessive opening of the medial knee and excessive inward angling of the knee. It supports medial stability during single-leg support and changes of direction and limits rotation.
A broad ligament along the inside of the knee that runs vertically between the femur and tibia.
Medial collateral ligament

Loaded during deadlifts, RDLs, supermans, bird dogs, and other movements that extend or stabilize the lower back. Load may increase when weight is supported at end-range lumbar extension or when extension and rotation are repeatedly combined.
Guides motion during lumbar extension and rotation and helps limit excessive front-to-back translation between vertebrae. It also shares pressure generated during back extension.
Small joints on both sides of the posterior lower lumbar spine, just above the pelvis, where adjacent vertebrae meet.
Lumbar facet joint
